Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 112, verses 1–4 (part 1 of 2):

Meccan. It has forty-seven letters, fifteen words, and four verses.

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Isfahani informed us, with me reading to him, saying: Abu Muhammad Abdullah ibn Ja'far ibn Ahmad ibn Faris informed us, saying: Yunus ibn Habib narrated to us, saying: Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: I heard Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd narrate from Ma'dan ibn Abi Talha, from Abu al-Darda', that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Is any of you unable to recite a third of the Qur'an in a night?" I said: "O Messenger of Allah, who is able to do that?" He said: "Recite ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾" [305] [[Musnad Ahmad: 6/442.]]

Abu Abdullah al-Husayn Muhammad ibn al-Faraj informed me, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Zayarqan narrated to us, saying: Marwan ibn Salim narrated to us, from Abu Umar, the client of Jarir ibn Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites it when he enters his house, it removes poverty from the people of that house and its neighbours." [306] [[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 10/128.]]

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Saqlab narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi al-Khasib narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: Sa'id ibn al-Mughira narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Marwan narrated to us, from Aban, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ once, he is blessed. Whoever recites it twice, he and his family are blessed. If he recites it three times, he, his family, and all his neighbours are blessed. If he recites it twelve times, twelve palaces are built for him in Paradise, and the angels who record deeds say: 'Come, let us go and look at the palace of our brother.' If he recites it a hundred times, the sins of twenty-five years are expiated for him, except for blood and property. If he recites it four hundred times, the sins of four hundred years are expiated for him, except for blood and property. If he recites it a thousand times, he will not die until he sees his place in Paradise, or it is shown to him." [307] [[In full in Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/479.]]

Abu Amr Ahmad ibn Abi al-Furati informed us, saying: Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Jami' al-Halwani narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Abbas narrated to us, saying: Umar ibn Sa'd al-Attar al-Falzami narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Dhi'b narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ghaylan narrated to us, from Abu Hazim, from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and complained to him of poverty and straitened livelihood. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "When you enter your house, greet whoever is in it, and if no one is in it, greet me [[Not present in the source.]] and recite ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ once." The man did so, and Allah granted him abundant provision, to the point that it overflowed to his neighbours. [308] [[Tafsir Nur al-Thaqalayn: 5/705.]]

Abu al-Husayn Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn Yahya informed us, saying: Abu Sa'id Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ziyad ibn Bishr narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabah al-Za'farani narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: al-Ala' Abu Muhammad al-Thaqafi narrated to us, saying: I heard Anas ibn Malik say: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Tabuk when the sun rose with a brightness, a radiance, and a light that I had not seen rise before. Jibril came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Jibril, why do I see the sun rise today with brightness, light, and radiance, which I have never seen before?' He said: 'That is because Mu'awiya ibn Mu'awiya al-Layth died today in Madina. Allah sent to him seventy thousand angels who pray over him.' He said: 'And why is that?' He said: 'He used to recite ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ much, by night and by day, while walking, standing, and sitting. Would you like, O Messenger of Allah, that I fold up the earth for you so that you may pray over him?' He said: 'Yes.'" [309] [[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 9/377.]] So he prayed over him and then returned.

Ahmad ibn Abi informed us, saying: Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Minqari narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Aziz ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Abdullah ibn Umar, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas ibn Malik, that a man used to pray during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and whenever he recited in the prayer he would recite ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ right after it. This was mentioned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to him: "What made you persist in it?" He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I love it." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Your love for it will admit you into Paradise." [310] [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 4/243, with slight variation.]]

Naqil ibn Raqim ibn Ahmad al-Babi informed us, saying: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Bakhtiyar narrated to us, saying: Abu Ibrahim al-Qattan narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Abdullah al-Qurashi narrated to us, saying: Salama ibn Sinan narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "An angel descended from the seventh heaven, and an angel emerged from the seventh earth, and they met on this earth. The one who had descended from the heaven said: 'Today I have raised a deed the like of which I have never raised.' The one who had come out from beneath the earth said: 'What is that?' He said: 'A man recited ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ a hundred times.' He said: 'What did Allah do with him?' He said: 'Allah forgave him.'" [311]

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim informed me, saying: Muhammad ibn Yazid narrated to us, saying: Abu Yahya al-Bazzaz narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Azhar narrated to us, saying: Abu Amir al-Aqadi narrated to us, from Malik ibn Anas, from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Ibn Jubayr, from Abu Hurayra, that the Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man reciting ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ and said: "It is due (wajabat)." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is due?" He said: "Paradise is due to him." [312] [[Musnad Ahmad: 2/302.]]

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim informed me, saying: Abu al-Qasim Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn al-Dasht narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Quraysh narrated to us, saying: Mu'adh ibn Yusuf al-Tajir narrated to us, saying: Musaddad ibn Musarhad narrated to us, saying: Hamdan ibn Razzam narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abdullah narrated to us, from Malik ibn Dinar, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ once, Allah grants him a reward whose weight would be seventy qintars of rubies, and its fragrance will spread out. They will carry his books as a single book, more pleasing to the touch than the hair of the Zanj and softer than hair." [313]

Muhammad ibn al-Qasim informed me, saying: Abu Muhammad Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Abu Hassan al-Uthmani informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: My paternal uncle Abdullah ibn Wahb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Lahi'a narrated to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir, from Makhul, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Prophet (peace be upon him) was asked about the reward for ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ and he said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ goodness will scatter upon the crown of his head from the clouds of the sky, tranquility will descend upon him, the Merciful will cover him, and he will be drawn around the Throne. Allah, glorified is He, will look upon its reciter, and He will not be asked for anything except that He gives it, and He will place him in His protection and safeguard." [314]

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾

Shaykh Abu Tahir Muhammad ibn al-Fadl ibn Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Muzakki informed us, saying: The Imam Abu Badr Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzayma informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Mani' and Mahmud ibn Khadash narrated to us, both saying: Abu Sa'd al-Saghani narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far al-Razi narrated to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliya, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that the polytheists said to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him): "Describe your Lord to us," so Allah, glorified is He, revealed ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One.﴾ to the end of the surah.

Abu Dabyan and Abu Salih related from Ibn Abbas that Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'a came to the Prophet (ﷺ). Amir said: "To what do you call us, O Muhammad?" He said: "To Allah, glorified is He." They said: "Describe Him to us. Is He of gold, silver, iron, or wood?" So this surah was revealed. Allah, glorified is He, sent a thunderbolt upon Arbad and it burned him, and Amir was stabbed in his little finger and died. Their story has been mentioned in Surat al-Ra'd.

Al-Dahhak, Qatada, and Muqatil said: Some of the rabbis of the Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, describe your Lord to us, that perhaps we may believe in you. Allah has sent down His description in the Torah, so inform us of it: of what substance is He? Is He of gold, copper, brass, iron, or silver? Does He eat and drink? From whom did He inherit the world? And who will inherit it from Him?" So Allah, glorified is He, revealed this surah, which is the lineage of Allah specifically.

Al-Abbas ibn Abi Rafi'... [see note below]

Aqil informed me that Abu Faraj al-Baghdadi informed them, from Abu Ja'far al-Tarafi, who said: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn Sa'id, who said: A group of Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, this Allah created creation; then who created Him?" The Prophet became angry until his face turned pale. Then he rose in anger for the sake of his Lord. Jibril came to him, calmed him, and said: "Lower your wing over yourself, O Muhammad." Allah sent him an answer to what they had asked: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, the surah. When the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to them, they said to him: "Describe your Lord to us: how He created, and how His arm and forearm are?" The Prophet (ﷺ) became angrier than his first anger and rose up against them. Jibril came to him and said to him the like of his previous words, and brought him an answer to what they had asked: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection﴾. [[Surat al-Zumar: 67.]]

Al-Dahhak said, from Ibn Abbas: The delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), seven bishops from the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, among them al-Sayyid and al-Aqib. They said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Describe your Lord to us: of what substance is He?"

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My Lord is not of any substance, and He is separate from the creation of things." [315] [[In Subul al-Huda by al-Shami (3/396): "He is separate from the creators of things."]] So Allah, glorified is He, revealed ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, meaning: the one (wahid).

There is no difference between wahid and ahad according to most of our companions, as evidenced by the reading of Abdullah: "Say: He is Allah [ ... ]" [[Blank space in the manuscript copy.]]

Another group distinguished between them. Some of them said: wahid is for separation, and ahad is for the extreme limit. It was said: wahid in His attributes, ahad in His essence. It was said: wahid indicates His eternity and primordiality, because wahid is the foundation, origin, and basis of numbers. Ahad indicates His distinction from His creation in all attributes and the negation of the gates of association from Him. So ahad was established to negate what is mentioned with it of number, while wahid is a name for the beginning of number. Thus ahad is suitable in speech in a context of denial, while wahid is in a context of affirmation. You say: "No one (ahad) came to me from them," and "One (wahid) came to me from them," meaning: two did not come to me.

Ibn al-Anbari said: I find in the original "wahid," as they said for a woman "anat," the original being "wanat," from weariness, which is lassitude. The poet said:

She was struck by a languid woman of the Rabi'a, of Amir,
Sleeping through the forenoon in a mourning gathering, what a gathering!

[[Al-Sihah: 5/1857.]]

Al-Nabigha said about the wahid:

As if my saddle, when the day departed with us,
At Dhu al-Jalil, upon a companionable wild ass of the wilderness.

[[Taj al-'Arus: 7/261.]]

I heard Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn Abdullah say: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Bazzaz say: I heard Ibn Ata' say concerning His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾: He is the one who alone brings the nonexistent into existence, and the one united in manifesting the hidden things.

The common reading is ahadun with tanwin. Al-Hasan, Nasr ibn Asim, Ibn Ishaq, Aban ibn Uthman, and Harun ibn Isa read "Ahadu Allah" without tanwin, seeking lightness and avoiding the meeting of two unvocalized letters, like the reading of those who read ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾ [[Surat al-Tawba: 30.]] without tanwin.

As for His saying ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾, they differed concerning it. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is the one who has no hollow (jawf). As for Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: the one who has no inner filling (hashw). Al-Sha'bi: the one who does not eat or drink, and al-Farradi went to this. It was said: "What follows it makes it an exception (yaftaruhu ma ba'dahu)."

Muhammad ibn al-Fadl informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzayma informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Mani' and Mahmud ibn Khurash narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'd al-Sa'bali narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far al-Razi narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliya, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "The Eternal Refuge is the one who did not beget and was not begotten, because there is nothing born except that it will die, and there is nothing that inherits except that it will be inherited, while Allah does not die and is not inherited."

Abu Wa'il Shaqiq ibn Salama said: He is the lord whose lordship has reached its end. This is the narration of Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, who said: He is the lord who has perfected every kind of nobility and lordship.

Others said: He is the lord to whom one turns with needs. The Arabs say: "I aimed at (sammadtu) so-and-so, I aim at him (asmaduhu), and aiming (samadan) with the m sukun," when one intends him. The "maṣmūd" is "ṣamad," like "qabḍ" and "nafḍ." It is said: "a house that is maṣmūd or muṣammad," when people come to it with their needs. Tarafa said:

And when the whole tribe meets, they meet me
At the summit of the lofty, sought-after house.

[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/483.]]

The scholars recited about al-Samad:

Did the mourner announce my good news to the Banu Asad,
Concerning Amr ibn Mas'ud and the lord al-Samad?

[[Lisan al-'Arab: 3/258.]]

Qatada said: al-Samad is the one who remains after His creation. 'Asim and Ma'mar said: He is the everlasting.

Ali ibn Musa al-Rida said: He is the one whose manner intellects have despaired of comprehending.

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: He is the eternal without number, the enduring without limit, and the upholder without pillars. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: He is the eternal without beginning. It was said: He is the one who is exalted above the likeness of the formers. It was said: it means the negation of division and composition from His essence. Maysara: the solid. Ibn Mas'ud: the one who has no inner parts.

Abu Ishaq al-Kufi, from Ikrima: al-Samad is the one above whom there is no one, and this is the saying of Ali, peace be upon him.

Al-Suddi: He is the one to whom one turns in desires and is sought for help at calamities. Yaman: the one who does not sleep. Ka'b al-Ahbar: the one whom none of His creation equals. Ibn Kaysan: the one whom no one can describe by His attributes. Muqatil ibn Hayyan: the one in whom there is no defect. Rabi': the one who is not affected by calamities. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: the perfect in all His attributes and actions. Al-Sadiq: He is the overpowering one who cannot be overpowered. Abu Hurayra: the one who needs no one, and to whom everyone is in need. Murra al-Hamdani: the one who does not decay and does not perish. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl also said: He is the one who decides what He wills and does what He pleases ... there is no one to reverse His judgment and no one to repel His decree.

Muhammad ibn Ali: al-Samad is the one whom eyes do not perceive, whom thoughts do not contain, whom regions do not reach, and "everything with Him is by measure." [[Cf. Qur'an 13:8.]]

Ibn Ata': al-Samad is the one in whom no trace is evident in what He manifests.

Ja'far: the one who has given His creatures from His knowledge only the name and the attribute.

Junayd: the one who has not allowed His enemies a path to knowing Him. It was said: He is the one whose true descriptions and attributes cannot be grasped, so the tongue cannot encompass Him and expression cannot point to Him. Ibn Ata': He is the one exalted above existence and corruption. Al-Wasiti said: the one who is not bewitched, not overwhelmed, and against whom no obstacles or impediments can prevail.

Ja'far also said: al-Samad has five letters. The alif is a proof of His oneness, and the lam is a proof of His divinity. These two are assimilated and do not appear on the tongue, but appear in writing. Thus it indicates His oneness and divinity in a hidden way that is not perceived by the senses, and that He cannot be measured by people. Its hiddenness in pronunciation is evidence that intellects cannot grasp Him or encompass Him in knowledge, and its manifestation in writing is evidence that He appears to the hearts of the knowers and becomes visible to the eyes of the lovers in the Abode of Peace. The sad is a proof of His truthfulness: His promise is true, His word is true, His act is true, and He calls His servants to truthfulness. The mim is a proof of His sovereignty, so He is the King in truth. The dal is a sign of His permanence in His everlastingness and eternity.

﴿He neither begets nor is born, and there is none comparable to Him.﴾ The readers differed concerning it. Hamza and Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the fa' and with hamza, and similarly al-Abbas related from Abu Amr, and Isma'il from Nafi'. Shayba read it with an elongated vowel without hamza, and similarly Hafs related from 'Asim. The others read it with a heavy stress and hamza. All of them are correct and eloquent dialects, and its meaning is "equal" (mithl).

Ahad means "He is one." It was said: it is in front-and-back order, its sense being: "and there was not to Him any one equal."

Abd Khayr said: A man asked Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, about the tafsir of this surah. He said: "﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ without the interpretation of number. ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ who is not divided into parts. ﴿He neither begets﴾, so He would be perishing, ﴿nor is He begotten﴾, so He would be a god sharing (divinity). ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ of His creation, ﴿One.﴾" [316] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/489.]]

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami related to us, with my reading to him, saying: I heard Abu Bakr al-Razi say: I heard Abu 'Ali al-Rudhbari say: "We have found the types of shirk (associating partners with God) to be eight: deficiency, change, multiplicity, number, being a cause or being an effect, shapes, and opposites. God, exalted is He, negated from His attributes the type of multiplicity and number by His saying: ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾. He negated deficiency and change by His saying: ﴿God, the Eternal Refuge﴾. He negated causes and effects by His saying: ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾. He negated shapes and opposites by His saying: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾. Thus the pure Oneness was established, and for this reason it was named Surat al-Ikhlas (the Chapter of Sincerity)."

There is no difference between wahid and ahad according to most of our companions, as evidenced by the reading of Abdullah: "Say: He is Allah [ ... ]" [[Blank space in the manuscript copy.]]

Another group distinguished between them. Some of them said: wahid is for separation, and ahad is for the extreme limit. It was said: wahid in His attributes, ahad in His essence. It was said: wahid indicates His eternity and primordiality, because wahid is the foundation, origin, and basis of numbers. Ahad indicates His distinction from His creation in all attributes and the negation of the gates of association from Him. So ahad was established to negate what is mentioned with it of number, while wahid is a name for the beginning of number. Thus ahad is suitable in speech in a context of denial, while wahid is in a context of affirmation. You say: "No one (ahad) came to me from them," and "One (wahid) came to me from them," meaning: two did not come to me.

Ibn al-Anbari said: I find in the original "wahid," as they said for a woman "anat," the original being "wanat," from weariness, which is lassitude. The poet said:

She was struck by a languid woman of the Rabi'a, of Amir,
Sleeping through the forenoon in a mourning gathering, what a gathering!

[[Al-Sihah: 5/1857.]]

Al-Nabigha said about the wahid:

As if my saddle, when the day departed with us,
At Dhu al-Jalil, upon a companionable wild ass of the wilderness.

I heard Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn Abdullah say: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Bazzaz say: I heard Ibn Ata' say concerning His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾: He is the one who alone brings the nonexistent into existence, and the one united in manifesting the hidden things.

The common reading is ahadun with tanwin. Al-Hasan, Nasr ibn Asim, Ibn Ishaq, Aban ibn Uthman, and Harun ibn Isa read "Ahadu Allah" without tanwin, seeking lightness and avoiding the meeting of two unvocalized letters, like the reading of those who read ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾ [[Surat al-Tawba: 30.]] without tanwin.

As for His saying ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾, they differed concerning it. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is the one who has no hollow (jawf). As for Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: the one who has no inner filling (hashw). Al-Sha'bi: the one who does not eat or drink, and al-Farradi went to this. Others said: He is the lord to whom one turns with needs. The Arabs say: "I aimed at (sammadtu) so-and-so, I aim at him (asmaduhu), and aiming (samadan) with the m sukun," when one intends him. And when the whole tribe meets, they meet me
At the summit of the lofty, sought-after house.

[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/483.]]

Did the mourner announce my good news to the Banu Asad,
Concerning Amr ibn Mas'ud and the lord al-Samad?

[[Lisan al-'Arab: 3/258.]]

Qatada said: al-Samad is the one who remains after His creation. 'Asim and Ma'mar said: He is the everlasting.

Ali ibn Musa al-Rida said: He is the one whose manner intellects have despaired of comprehending.

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: He is the eternal without number, the enduring without limit, and the upholder without pillars. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: He is the eternal without beginning. It was said: He is the one who is exalted above the likeness of the formers. It was said: it means the negation of division and composition from His essence. Maysara: the solid. Ibn Mas'ud: the one who has no inner parts.

Abu Ishaq al-Kufi, from Ikrima: al-Samad is the one above whom there is no one, and this is the saying of Ali, peace be upon him.

Al-Suddi: He is the one to whom one turns in desires and is sought for help at calamities. Yaman: the one who does not sleep. Ka'b al-Ahbar: the one whom none of His creation equals. Ibn Kaysan: the one whom no one can describe by His attributes. Muqatil ibn Hayyan: the one in whom there is no defect. Rabi': the one who is not affected by calamities. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: the perfect in all His attributes and actions. Al-Sadiq: He is the overpowering one who cannot be overpowered. Abu Hurayra: the one who needs no one, and to whom everyone is in need. Murra al-Hamdani: the one who does not decay and does not perish. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl also said: He is the one who decides what He wills and does what He pleases ... there is no one to reverse His judgment and no one to repel His decree.

Muhammad ibn Ali: al-Samad is the one whom eyes do not perceive, whom thoughts do not contain, whom regions do not reach, and "everything with Him is by measure." [[Cf. Qur'an 13:8.]]

Ibn Ata': al-Samad is the one in whom no trace is evident in what He manifests.

Ja'far: the one who has given His creatures from His knowledge only the name and the attribute.

Junayd: the one who has not allowed His enemies a path to knowing Him. It was said: He is the one whose true descriptions and attributes cannot be grasped, so the tongue cannot encompass Him and expression cannot point to Him. Ibn Ata': He is the one exalted above existence and corruption. Al-Wasiti said: the one who is not bewitched, not overwhelmed, and against whom no obstacles or impediments can prevail.

Ja'far also said: al-Samad has five letters. The alif is a proof of His oneness, and the lam is a proof of His divinity. These two are assimilated and do not appear on the tongue, but appear in writing. Thus it indicates His oneness and divinity in a hidden way that is not perceived by the senses, and that He cannot be measured by people. Its hiddenness in pronunciation is evidence that intellects cannot grasp Him or encompass Him in knowledge, and its manifestation in writing is evidence that He appears to the hearts of the knowers and becomes visible to the eyes of the lovers in the Abode of Peace. The sad is a proof of His truthfulness: His promise is true, His word is true, His act is true, and He calls His servants to truthfulness. The mim is a proof of His sovereignty, so He is the King in truth. The dal is a sign of His permanence in His everlastingness and eternity.

﴿He neither begets nor is born, and there is none comparable to Him.﴾ The readers differed concerning it. Hamza and Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the fa' and with hamza, and similarly al-Abbas related from Abu Amr, and Isma'il from Nafi'. Shayba read it with an elongated vowel without hamza, and similarly Hafs related from 'Asim. The others read it with a heavy stress and hamza. All of them are correct and eloquent dialects, and its meaning is "equal" (mithl).

Ahad means "He is one." It was said: it is in front-and-back order, its sense being: "and there was not to Him any one equal."

God, exalted is He, negated from His attributes the type of multiplicity and number by His saying: ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾. He negated deficiency and change by His saying: ﴿God, the Eternal Refuge﴾. He negated causes and effects by His saying: ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾. He negated shapes and opposites by His saying: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾. Thus the pure Oneness was established, and for this reason it was named Surat al-Ikhlas (the Chapter of Sincerity)."

Another group distinguished between them. Some of them said: wahid is for separation, and ahad is for the extreme limit. It was said: wahid in His attributes, ahad in His essence. It was said: wahid indicates His eternity and primordiality, because wahid is the foundation, origin, and basis of numbers. Ahad indicates His distinction from His creation in all attributes and the negation of the gates of association from Him. So ahad was established to negate what is mentioned with it of number, while wahid is a name for the beginning of number. Thus ahad is suitable in speech in a context of denial, while wahid is in a context of affirmation. You say: "No one (ahad) came to me from them," and "One (wahid) came to me from them," meaning: two did not come to me.

Ibn al-Anbari said: I find in the original "wahid," as they said for a woman "anat," the original being "wanat," from weariness, which is lassitude. The poet said:

She was struck by a languid woman of the Rabi'a, of Amir,
Sleeping through the forenoon in a mourning gathering, what a gathering!

[[Al-Sihah: 5/1857.]]

Al-Nabigha said about the wahid:

As if my saddle, when the day departed with us,
At Dhu al-Jalil, upon a companionable wild ass of the wilderness.

[[Taj al-'Arus: 7/261.]]

I heard Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami say: I heard Mansur ibn Abdullah say: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Bazzaz say: I heard Ibn Ata' say concerning His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾: He is the one who alone brings the nonexistent into existence, and the one united in manifesting the hidden things.

The common reading is ahadun with tanwin. Al-Hasan, Nasr ibn Asim, Ibn Ishaq, Aban ibn Uthman, and Harun ibn Isa read "Ahadu Allah" without tanwin, seeking lightness and avoiding the meeting of two unvocalized letters, like the reading of those who read ﴿Uzayr is the son of Allah﴾ [[Surat al-Tawba: 30.]] without tanwin.

As for His saying ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾, they differed concerning it. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is the one who has no hollow (jawf). As for Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: the one who has no inner filling (hashw). Al-Sha'bi: the one who does not eat or drink, and al-Farradi went to this. It was said: "What follows it makes it an exception (yaftaruhu ma ba'dahu)."

Muhammad ibn al-Fadl informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzayma informed us, saying: Ahmad ibn Mani' and Mahmud ibn Khurash narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'd al-Sa'bali narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far al-Razi narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliya, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "The Eternal Refuge is the one who did not beget and was not begotten, because there is nothing born except that it will die, and there is nothing that inherits except that it will be inherited, while Allah does not die and is not inherited."

Others said: He is the lord to whom one turns with needs. The Arabs say: "I aimed at (sammadtu) so-and-so, I aim at him (asmaduhu), and aiming (samadan) with the m sukun," when one intends him. The "maṣmūd" is "ṣamad," like "qabḍ" and "nafḍ." It is said: "a house that is maṣmūd or muṣammad," when people come to it with their needs. Tarafa said:

And when the whole tribe meets, they meet me
At the summit of the lofty, sought-after house.

[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/483.]]

The scholars recited about al-Samad:

Did the mourner announce my good news to the Banu Asad,
Concerning Amr ibn Mas'ud and the lord al-Samad?

[[Lisan al-'Arab: 3/258.]]

Qatada said: al-Samad is the one who remains after His creation. 'Asim and Ma'mar said: He is the everlasting.

Ali ibn Musa al-Rida said: He is the one whose manner intellects have despaired of comprehending.

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: He is the eternal without number, the enduring without limit, and the upholder without pillars. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: He is the eternal without beginning. It was said: He is the one who is exalted above the likeness of the formers. It was said: it means the negation of division and composition from His essence. Maysara: the solid. Ibn Mas'ud: the one who has no inner parts.

Abu Ishaq al-Kufi, from Ikrima: al-Samad is the one above whom there is no one, and this is the saying of Ali, peace be upon him.

Al-Suddi: He is the one to whom one turns in desires and is sought for help at calamities. Yaman: the one who does not sleep. Ka'b al-Ahbar: the one whom none of His creation equals. Ibn Kaysan: the one whom no one can describe by His attributes. Muqatil ibn Hayyan: the one in whom there is no defect. Rabi': the one who is not affected by calamities. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: the perfect in all His attributes and actions. Al-Sadiq: He is the overpowering one who cannot be overpowered. Abu Hurayra: the one who needs no one, and to whom everyone is in need. Murra al-Hamdani: the one who does not decay and does not perish. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl also said: He is the one who decides what He wills and does what He pleases ... there is no one to reverse His judgment and no one to repel His decree.

Muhammad ibn Ali: al-Samad is the one whom eyes do not perceive, whom thoughts do not contain, whom regions do not reach, and "everything with Him is by measure." [[Cf. Qur'an 13:8.]]

Ibn Ata': al-Samad is the one in whom no trace is evident in what He manifests.

Ja'far: the one who has given His creatures from His knowledge only the name and the attribute.

Junayd: the one who has not allowed His enemies a path to knowing Him. It was said: He is the one whose true descriptions and attributes cannot be grasped, so the tongue cannot encompass Him and expression cannot point to Him. Ibn Ata': He is the one exalted above existence and corruption. Al-Wasiti said: the one who is not bewitched, not overwhelmed, and against whom no obstacles or impediments can prevail.

Ja'far also said: al-Samad has five letters. The alif is a proof of His oneness, and the lam is a proof of His divinity. These two are assimilated and do not appear on the tongue, but appear in writing. Thus it indicates His oneness and divinity in a hidden way that is not perceived by the senses, and that He cannot be measured by people. Its hiddenness in pronunciation is evidence that intellects cannot grasp Him or encompass Him in knowledge, and its manifestation in writing is evidence that He appears to the hearts of the knowers and becomes visible to the eyes of the lovers in the Abode of Peace. The sad is a proof of His truthfulness: His promise is true, His word is true, His act is true, and He calls His servants to truthfulness. The mim is a proof of His sovereignty, so He is the King in truth. The dal is a sign of His permanence in His everlastingness and eternity.

All of them are correct and eloquent dialects, and its meaning is "equal" (mithl).

Ahad means "He is one." It was said: it is in front-and-back order, its sense being: "and there was not to Him any one equal."

[306] [[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 10/128.]]

Whoever recites it twice, he and his family are blessed. If he recites it three times, he, his family, and all his neighbours are blessed. If he recites it four hundred times, the sins of four hundred years are expiated for him, except for blood and property. Ibn Ata': al-Samad is the one in whom no trace is evident in what He manifests.

Ja'far: the one who has given His creatures from His knowledge only the name and the attribute.

Junayd: the one who has not allowed His enemies a path to knowing Him. It was said: He is the one whose true descriptions and attributes cannot be grasped, so the tongue cannot encompass Him and expression cannot point to Him. Ibn Ata': He is the one exalted above existence and corruption. Al-Wasiti said: the one who is not bewitched, not overwhelmed, and against whom no obstacles or impediments can prevail.

Ja'far also said: al-Samad has five letters. The alif is a proof of His oneness, and the lam is a proof of His divinity. These two are assimilated and do not appear on the tongue, but appear in writing. Thus it indicates His oneness and divinity in a hidden way that is not perceived by the senses, and that He cannot be measured by people. Its hiddenness in pronunciation is evidence that intellects cannot grasp Him or encompass Him in knowledge, and its manifestation in writing is evidence that He appears to the hearts of the knowers and becomes visible to the eyes of the lovers in the Abode of Peace. The sad is a proof of His truthfulness: His promise is true, His word is true, His act is true, and He calls His servants to truthfulness. The mim is a proof of His sovereignty, so He is the King in truth. The dal is a sign of His permanence in His everlastingness and eternity.

﴿He neither begets nor is born, and there is none comparable to Him.﴾ The readers differed concerning it. Hamza and Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the fa' and with hamza, and similarly al-Abbas related from Abu Amr, and Isma'il from Nafi'. Shayba read it with an elongated vowel without hamza, and similarly Hafs related from 'Asim. The others read it with a heavy stress and hamza. All of them are correct and eloquent dialects, and its meaning is "equal" (mithl).

Ahad means "He is one." It was said: it is in front-and-back order, its sense being: "and there was not to Him any one equal."

Abd Khayr said: A man asked Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, about the tafsir of this surah. He said: "﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ without the interpretation of number. ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ who is not divided into parts. ﴿He neither begets﴾, so He would be perishing, ﴿nor is He begotten﴾, so He would be a god sharing (divinity). ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ of His creation, ﴿One.﴾" [316] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 10/489.]]

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami related to us, with my reading to him, saying: I heard Abu Bakr al-Razi say: I heard Abu 'Ali al-Rudhbari say: "We have found the types of shirk (associating partners with God) to be eight: deficiency, change, multiplicity, number, being a cause or being an effect, shapes, and opposites. God, exalted is He, negated from His attributes the type of multiplicity and number by His saying: ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾. He negated deficiency and change by His saying: ﴿God, the Eternal Refuge﴾. He negated causes and effects by His saying: ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾. He negated shapes and opposites by His saying: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾. Thus the pure Oneness was established, and for this reason it was named Surat al-Ikhlas (the Chapter of Sincerity)."
